title: Single Headed Attention RNN: Stop Thinking With Your Head

pages.title: The big idea
pages.subtitle: A one-person, one-GPU rebellion against scale

blocks.html: By 2019 the field had decided that progress in language modeling meant Transformers with many attention heads, billions of parameters, and clusters of GPUs. Stephen Merity — writing alone, with a famously irreverent voice — pushes back. His thesis: maybe we reached for all that machinery before checking whether we actually needed it.

His counter-proposal is the SHA-RNN: a Single Headed Attention RNN. Take a strong LSTM backbone, bolt on a single attention head (not eight, not sixteen), add a deliberately simple feed-forward block he calls the ‘Boom’ layer, and train the whole thing on one GPU in about a day.

The SHA-RNN reaches strong byte-level results on the enwik8 benchmark — competitive with far larger, multi-head Transformer models — while being something a single researcher can actually train and tinker with.

The paper is half serious model and half manifesto. The wit is the point: Merity is arguing, with jokes about Sesame-Street model names and tokenizers, that the community's reflex to throw compute at every problem deserves more scrutiny.

pages.title: Against scale-maximalism
pages.subtitle: Did we need all those heads?

blocks.html: The central worry is methodological. When a bigger model trained on more compute beats a smaller one, it is tempting to credit the architecture — the many heads, the clever attention variant — when the real cause may simply be scale. If you never run the small, careful baseline, you cannot tell which it was.

Merity's response is to be that baseline. By deliberately constraining himself to a single GPU and a single attention head, he asks: how far can an old-fashioned LSTM, modestly augmented, actually get? If the answer is ‘surprisingly far,’ then much of the field's complexity may be optional.

There is also an accessibility argument woven through the wit. Research that requires a data center excludes nearly everyone. A model one person can train overnight keeps the field open to individuals — and that, Merity argues, is worth defending.

pages.title: The SHA-RNN block
pages.subtitle: LSTM, one attention head, and a Boom

blocks.html: Each SHA-RNN layer is built from three pieces stacked together, with layer normalization holding them steady:

items: An LSTM as the recurrent backbone — the workhorse that carries state across the sequence, doing most of the heavy lifting.
A single attention head that lets the current position reach back into a memory of past states, retrieving relevant context without the cost of multi-head machinery.
A Boom feed-forward layer — Merity's deliberately cheap stand-in for the Transformer's large feed-forward block.

blocks.html: The bet is that an LSTM already captures most of what recurrence needs, so attention can be a lightweight assistant rather than the entire model. One head is enough when the recurrent state is doing the rest of the work.

pages.title: The Boom layer
pages.subtitle: Expand, then add the pieces back up

blocks.html: A standard Transformer feed-forward block expands a vector of size $H$ up to a much larger size (say $4H$) with one matrix and projects it back down with a second, separate matrix — two big weight matrices. Merity's ‘Boom’ layer keeps the expansion but throws away the second matrix.

It projects $H$ up to a vector of size $N \\cdot H$, then simply chops that into $N$ chunks and sums them to get back to size $H$. The ‘boom’ is the explosive expansion; the collapse is free, just an addition:

Read this as: expand to a big vector, slice it into $N$ equal blocks, and add the blocks together. Because there is no second weight matrix for the down-projection, the Boom layer uses roughly half the parameters and compute of the usual feed-forward block — a small, slightly cheeky efficiency win that is very much in the spirit of the paper.

pages.title: Competitive on enwik8, on one GPU
pages.subtitle: Bits-per-character without a data center

blocks.html: The benchmark is enwik8: model the first 100 million bytes of Wikipedia at the byte level, scored in bits-per-character (bpc) — lower is better. Byte-level modeling sidesteps tokenizer choices entirely, which Merity, no fan of tokenizers, clearly enjoys.

rows: approx. 52M params, single GPU, about a day

blocks.html: The headline is not that the SHA-RNN wins — it is that it lands in the same neighborhood as much heavier models while being trainable on hardware a single researcher owns. With one attention head and a humble LSTM, it gets most of the way there. That is the whole argument made concrete.

History went the other way: scale kept paying off, and Transformers won. But the SHA-RNN remains a valuable check on the field's instincts. It is a reminder to run the careful small baseline before crediting an architecture, and to ask whether complexity is doing real work or just riding along with compute.

Its tone matters too. By making the case with humor — mocking model-naming fads, tokenizers, and compute-bragging — Merity made an efficiency-and-accessibility argument that people actually read and remembered. In an era of ever-larger models, the SHA-RNN is the field's most quotable footnote: a one-person, one-GPU model that asked everyone to stop thinking with their heads.
